doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: First European tour with Lena, mistaken for Martinique, Congo and India
summary: On the first European tour, French press confusion led audiences in Paris, Belgium and England to mistake him for hated colonial peoples, and he was treated badly.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: well the Lady was cool, man. You know, she was cool, man. I felt sorry for her though man, because she had her luck with men. She had some crunchy men, man. She got all the bad dudes, man, bad dudes. You know, take advantage of her, you know. But we got along good. We got along. You know, that’s the only thing you can do, you know, when you play for a lady singer. As long as you keep that distance it was cool, you know. Otherwise man it becomes a drag. Unfortunately man, at that period man, during that period I was making good dough and that’s why I was there, you know that type of thing. The year, what was it, ‘50, I guess it was ‘50, ‘51, whatever year that was, I decided I wouldn’t go to Europe. Oh, first time I went to Europe with Lena, the French press made a mistake. They said Lena had a French drummer but we had a French bass player, Monsieur Pierre Michelot. And they thought -- so subsequently man, everywhere we went man in Europe I got a bad time. In Paris, they thought I was Martinique and they hate them. In Belgium they thought I was from the Congo, they hate them. In England they thought I was Indian, they hate -­
You were hated for all the wrong reasons.
Oh, man. I used to have to wear my passport. At first it was funny but after a while it got to be a drag.
You said they hated you. They were so open as far as their hostility?
Their hostility towards those people. You know, they were their subjects, Belgian Congo.
And you want to know something, I looked like all of them.
Uh-huh, that will do it. As do I, we look the same.
I look like I could be any one of them and it was -­
Rough, because especially to be over there in 1950 and not being in uniform because they had the select duty over there -- was in uniform, you know. You know, dap street clothes but anyway that’s -­
So what year did you go over with her that first time?
How long were you over there?
If I knew. I guess we were over there four or five months, something like that. And we sailed, we sailed on the -­
When you got there, you traveled by train?
